questions.html:
For Quick-Sort, let $\operatorname{comps}(n)$ be the number of comparisons required to sort $n$ elements, where each partition step performs $n-1$ comparisons.

Consider the following recurrences:

1. $\operatorname{comps}(n)=2 \cdot \operatorname{comps}(n / 2)+(n-1)$

2. $\operatorname{comps}(n)=\operatorname{comps}(n-1)+(n-1)$

Which of the following statements are true?

options.html: Recurrence ($1$) leads to $O(n \log n)$ comparisons, and this happens when the pivot always splits the array into two equal halves.
Recurrence ($2$) leads to $O\left(n^{2}\right)$ comparisons, and this happens when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element.
Recurrence ($1$) arises when the array is already sorted.
Recurrence ($2$) arises when the pivot is always the median of the current array.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 1)

These are the two recurrence relations of quicksort given in the question

 

1. comps(n)=2⋅comps(n/2)+(n−1)
2. comps(n)=comps(n−1)+(n−1)

Understand that the question is about Quicksort and each recurrence relation depicts how the array get's divided for further partitioning. For first recurrence relation : the pivot should be a median, and the second one : the pivot should either be the largest or the smallest element in the array

A. Is correct, master's theorem will give you the result O(nLogn).

B. T(n) = T(n-1) + n gives a complexity of O(n^2) by iteration method therefore true

C.Whether a sorted array leads to recurrence (1) depends on the pivot rule. If you pick first/last as pivot on a sorted array, you get the worst-case recurrence (2). A sorted array only gives recurrence (1) if the pivot choice produces balanced splits (e.g., always choosing the true median). Hence C is False.

D. D is False, because if Pivot was the median it would have take O(nlog n) and not O(n^2) as in Recurrence 2. The median produces balanced splits and recurrence (1). Recurrence (2) corresponds to extremely unbalanced pivots (min or max).

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

A — True. 

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + (n−1) = Θ(nlog⁡n)

The (n−1) comparisons are the total per level, and there are log⁡n levels.
This happens when the pivot is the median each time.

B — True.

Worst case gives

T(n) = T(n−1)+(n−1)
=(n−1)+(n−2)+⋯+1
=Θ(n2)

This occurs when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element.. 

C — False.

 A sorted array with a first/last pivot follows recurrence (2), not (1).

D — False.

If the pivot is always the median, that’s recurrence (1), not (2).

Consider the number of element swaps performed by selection sort and bubble sort in the worst case for a list of size $N$.

Which of the following statements are correct?

options.html: Selection sort always performs exactly ( $N-1$ ) element swaps.
The number of element swaps in selection sort depends on the initial arrangement of elements.
Bubble sort, in the worst case, performs $\frac{(N-2)(N-1)}{2}$ element swaps.
Bubble sort performs the same number of element swaps for both sorted and reverse-sorted arrays.

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

  • A $\checkmark \rightarrow$ True, classic selection sort does one swap per pass.

 

  • B $╳$  Check option A above

 

  • C $╳$ Worst-case bubble sort swaps $=$ comparisons $=\frac{N(N-1)}{2}$.

 

  • D $╳$   Sorted $\rightarrow 0$ swaps, reverse sorted $\rightarrow$ maximum swaps.

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

The number of element swaps performed by selection sort and bubble sort in the worst case for a list of size N

B. If the elements are already sorted in the desired order, swapping won't be needed, but comparisons will be needed. There can be doubt over the fact that it is the worst case we are talking about, and in the worst case you won't have the array sorted in the desired format. But then again, the statement is true regardless of sorted or not. Therefore B is True.

C. This option assumes (n-1)(n-2)/2 as the O(n) of bubble sort.
Therefore O(n) = (n2−3n+2​)/2 ; which isn't equal to n(n-1)/2 :- the standard worst case of bubble sort
The difference between the two time complexities = −(n−1), which proves that (n2−3n+2​)/2 is off by 1 swap. Therefore Option C is incorrect

D. It does worst case for one and best case for the other. Therefore they don't have equal time complexity. D is incorrect

These were my reasonings, correct me if I am wrong. @Dvruo Classes @Dvruo Classes Support

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

void selectionSort(int arr[], int n) {
    int i, j, min_index, temp;

    for (i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        min_index = i;

        // Find the minimum element in the unsorted part
        for (j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (arr[j] < arr[min_index]) {
                min_index = j;
            }
        }

        // Swap the found minimum with the first element
        temp = arr[min_index];
        arr[min_index] = arr[i];
        arr[i] = temp;
    }
}

questions.html:
Consider the following array:
$$
12,18,27,35,46,58,72,85
$$
Which algorithm out of the following options uses the least number of comparisons (among the array elements) to sort the above array in ascending order?

options.html: Quicksort using the last element as pivot

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 6)

The given array is already sorted in ascending order. In selection sort, the number of comparisons does not depend on the order of input. It will always perform $(n-1)+(n-2)+\cdots+1=\frac{n(n-1)}{2} \in \Theta\left(n^{2}\right)$ comparisons.

In merge sort, the array is divided into halves and merged back, and even if it is sorted, merging requires comparisons. Therefore, the number of comparisons will always be $O(n \log n)$.

In insertion sort, when the array is already sorted, each element requires only one comparison with its predecessor. Hence, the total number of comparisons is $n-1 \in \Theta(n)$, with no swaps required.

In quicksort with the last element chosen as pivot, a sorted array gives the worst-case performance, leading to $O\left(n^{2}\right)$ comparisons.

Therefore, among the given algorithms, insertion sort performs the least number of comparisons.

Answer: C. Insertion Sort

questions.html:
You are given an array $A$ of $n$ distinct integers in sorted order. The task is to determine whether there exists an index $i$ such that $A[i]=i$.

Which of the following statements are correct?

options.html: A naive algorithm that checks every index runs in $O(n)$ time.
If all integers are non-negative ( $A[i] \geq 0$ ), the problem can be solved in $O(1)$ time.
If all integers are positive, then no valid index can exist.
The problem always requires $O(n)$ time, regardless of the input conditions.

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 9)

Option A: True


The naive method checks every index $\rightarrow O(n)$.

Option B: True


If all integers are non-negative ( $A[i] \geq 0$ ):

  • If $A[0]=0$, then index 0 works.


If $A[0]>0$, then since the array is sorted, all later values are even larger, so no index can work.

Hence, the answer can be found in $O(1)$.

Option C: True

If all integers are positive, then even the first element is at least 1.

For $i=0, A[0] \neq 0$.

For $i>0$, since $A[i]>0$ and the array is increasing, we always get $A[i]>i$.

Therefore, no index can satisfy $A[i]=i$.

Option D: False

The problem doesn't always need $O(n)$; faster solutions exist.

questions.html:
Professor Fiorina uses the following algorithm for merging $k$ sorted lists, each having $\frac{n}{k}$ elements:

  • She merges the first two lists using a linear-time merge procedure.
     
  • Then she merges the resulting list with the third list, then with the fourth, and so on, until all lists are merged into a single sorted list of $n$ elements.

What is the worst-case running time of this algorithm in terms of $n$ and $k$?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

  • Merging the first two lists takes $\frac{2 n}{k}$ time.

 

  • Merging the result with the third list takes $\frac{3 n}{k}$ time, and so on.

 

  • Total cost:


$$
T(n, k)=\frac{2 n}{k}+\frac{3 n}{k}+\cdots+\frac{k n}{k}=\frac{n}{k} \sum_{i=2}^{k} i=\frac{n(k+2)(k-1)}{2 k}=\Theta(n k)
$$

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

Problem Statement Analysis:

  • We have $k$ sorted lists.

  • Each list has $n/k$ elements.

  • The strategy is iterative: Merge List 1 and 2, then merge the result with List 3, then with List 4, and so on.

Step-by-Step Solution:

Let $m = n/k$ be the size of each initial list.

  1. Merge 1: Merge List 1 ($m$) and List 2 ($m$).

    • Cost $\propto$ Sum of sizes = $m + m = 2m$.

    • Resulting list size = $2m$.

  2. Merge 2: Merge Result 1 ($2m$) and List 3 ($m$).

    • Cost $\propto 2m + m = 3m$.

    • Resulting list size = $3m$.

  3. Merge 3: Merge Result 2 ($3m$) and List 4 ($m$).

    • Cost $\propto 3m + m = 4m$.

    • Resulting list size = $4m$.

  4. ... Merge $i$:

    • Cost $\propto (i+1)m$.

  5. Total Cost: We perform this $k-1$ times. The total time complexity is the sum of costs for all merges.

     

    $$T(n, k) = \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} (i+1)m$$

    $$T(n, k) = m(2 + 3 + \dots + k)$$

     

    The sum is an arithmetic progression roughly equal to $O(k^2)$.

     

    $$T(n, k) = m \cdot O(k^2)$$

  6. Substitute $m$:

    Since $m = n/k$:

     

    $$T(n, k) = \frac{n}{k} \cdot O(k^2) = O(nk)$$

Correct Option:

C. $\Theta(nk)$

 

 

Source solution 3 (score: 1)

So the answer is option C

questions.html:
Assume a variant of Quicksort in which, at every recursive step, the input array of size \(n\) is deterministically partitioned into two subproblems:

\[ \boxed{\;\;\;\underbrace{\phantom{xxxxxxxx}}_{\alpha n}\;\;\;\;\;\underbrace{\phantom{xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx}}_{(1-\alpha)n}\;\;\;} \]

where \(0 < \alpha \leq \tfrac{1}{2}\).

What is the asymptotic expression for the maximum depth of the recursion tree in terms of \(n\) and \(\alpha\)?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

$$
n \rightarrow(1-\alpha) n \rightarrow(1-\alpha)^{2} n \rightarrow(1-\alpha)^{3} n \rightarrow \ldots
$$

Recursion continues until the subproblem size becomes at most 1.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (1-\alpha)^{k} \cdot n \leq 1 \\
& (1-\alpha)^{k} \leq \frac{1}{n} \\
& k \cdot \lg (1-\alpha) \leq-\lg n
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $0<1-\alpha<1$, we know:
$$
\lg (1-\alpha)<0
$$

Dividing both sides by a negative flips the inequality:
$$
k \geq-\frac{\lg n}{\lg (1-\alpha)}
$$

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

 

 

Problem Statement Analysis:

We have a QuickSort variant where every step partitions an array of size $n$ into two parts:

  1. A smaller part of size $\alpha n$ (since $0 < \alpha \le 1/2$).

  2. A larger part of size $(1-\alpha)n$.

We need to find the maximum depth of the recursion tree.

Step-by-Step Solution:

  1. Understanding Tree Depth: The recursion tree branches out at each step. One branch processes the left partition, and the other processes the right. The "depth" of a specific leaf node is the number of splits (recursive calls) made to reach a subarray of size 1.

  2. Identifying the Longest Path: The maximum depth corresponds to the "worst-case" branch of the tree where the problem size decreases the slowest.

    • The problem size decreases faster along the branch of size $\alpha n$ (since $\alpha$ is the smaller fraction).

    • The problem size decreases slower along the branch of size $(1-\alpha)n$ (the larger fraction).

  3. Formulating the Equation: To find the maximum depth $d$, we assume we always take the largest branch. We stop when the array size reduces to 1.

     

    $$n \cdot (1 - \alpha)^d = 1$$

  4. Solving for $d$:

    Take the logarithm (base 2, denoted as $\lg$) on both sides:

     

    $$\lg(n \cdot (1-\alpha)^d) = \lg(1)$$

    $$\lg n + d \cdot \lg(1-\alpha) = 0$$

    $$d \cdot \lg(1-\alpha) = -\lg n$$

    $$d = \frac{-\lg n}{\lg(1-\alpha)} = -\frac{\lg n}{\lg(1-\alpha)}$$

    Note: Since $(1-\alpha)$ is less than 1, $\lg(1-\alpha)$ is a negative number. The negative sign in front makes the final depth positive, which is correct.

Correct Option:

A. $-\frac{\lg n}{\lg(1-\alpha)}$

 

Source solution 3 (score: 2)

Sol:

Source solution 4 (score: 0)

Maximum depth is achieved at the end of the part with the larger ratio.
Here, it will be (1−α) since 0 < α ≤ 1/2.
Example: if α=1/4 → the maximum depth will be at the end of 1−α, that is 3/4.

Now, T(n) = (1−α)n
T((1−α)n) = (1−α)(1−α)n   ....(replace n with (1−α)n),
and so on: T((1−α)^{k−1} n) = (1−α)^k n

So it will stop when (1−α)^k n <= 1,
i.e., (1−α)^k = 1/n.

Take logs on both sides. To find the depth, we need k:
k = log(1/n) / log(1−α)
  = log(n^{−1}) / log(1−α)
  = − log(n) / log(1−α).

Answer: A

questions.html:
Randomized QuickSort (where the pivot is chosen uniformly at random from the current subarray) is applied on an array of $10$ distinct numbers. Suppose we focus on the elements $25$ and $70$, which in the sorted order look like this:

$$10,18,22,25,31,40,53,66,70,85$$
What is the probability that $25$ and $70$ are directly compared at some stage of QuickSort?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 9)

Problem Statement Analysis:

  • Array elements (sorted): 10, 18, 22, 25, 31, 40, 53, 66, 70, 85.

  • We need the probability that 25 and 70 are compared.

Concept:

In Randomized QuickSort, two elements $x$ and $y$ are compared if and only if one of them is chosen as the pivot before any other element that lies numerically between them (in the sorted order). If an element between them is picked first, $x$ goes to the left subarray and $y$ to the right (or vice versa), and they are never compared.

Step-by-Step Solution:

  1. Identify the Range: Look at the sorted sequence and identify all elements between 25 and 70 (inclusive).

    Set $S = \{25, 31, 40, 53, 66, 70\}$.

  2. Count the Elements:

    There are 6 elements in this set: 25, 31, 40, 53, 66, 70.

  3. Calculate Probability:

    For 25 and 70 to be compared, the first pivot chosen from this specific set $S$ must be either 25 or 70.

    • Total candidates in set $S$ = 6.

    • Favorable candidates (25 or 70) = 2.

    • Probability = $\frac{\text{Favorable}}{\text{Total}} = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$.

Correct Option:

C. $1/3$

questions.html:
Consider the problem of sorting an array of size $n$ using only the following two operations:

$\operatorname{compare}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})$ : compares two elements $x$ and $y$.

flip(i): reverses the order of the first $i$ elements of the array.

For example, if the array is $[1,4,6,5,3,10,1]$, then applying flip(4) results in $[5,6,4,1,3,10,1]$.

The Pancake Sort algorithm works as follows:

In each iteration,

  • find the maximum element in the current prefix of size $k$,
     
  • flip the prefix to bring this maximum element to the front (if needed),
     
  • flip the first $k$ elements to move the maximum into its correct final position at index $k$.

This process is repeated for $k=n, n-1, \ldots, 2$.

Which of the following statements is/are correct about Pancake Sort?

options.html: After the $i$-th iteration, the last $i$ elements of the array are in their correct sorted positions.
In each iteration, the algorithm always requires exactly 1 flip in the worst case.
In the worst case, the total number of flips performed by the algorithm is at most $2 n$.
The number of comparisons required by the algorithm is $O\left(n^{2}\right)$.

Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

$\mathbf{Option A: True}$

Each iteration ensures that the maximum element of the current prefix is placed in its correct position at the end. Hence, after the $i$-th iteration, the last $i$ elements are correctly placed.

$\mathbf{Option B: False}$

In the worst case, an iteration may require 2 flips (one to bring the maximum to the front, another to move it to the end). It is not always just 1 flip.

$\mathbf{Option C: True}$

There are ( $n-1$ ) iterations, each needing at most 2 flips. Therefore, the worst-case total number of flips is $2 n-2<2 n$.

$\mathbf{Option D: True}$

Finding the maximum in each prefix of length $k$ requires $O(k)$ comparisons. Summing over all iterations:

$$
O(n+(n-1)+\cdots+2)=O\left(n^{2}\right)
$$

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Based on the analysis of the Pancake Sort algorithm described, here is the evaluation of each statement:

1. Algorithm Analysis

The algorithm described is essentially a variation of Selection Sort. In each pass, it selects the maximum element from the unsorted prefix and moves it to its correct position at the end of the prefix using reversal operations (flip).

  • Comparisons: In each iteration with prefix size $k$, finding the maximum element requires scanning the array, which takes $k-1$ comparisons.

  • Flips: To move an element to position $k$, we typically perform two flips:

    1. Flip the prefix ending at the maximum element (to bring it to the front).

    2. Flip the prefix of size $k$ (to move it from the front to position $k$).

2. Evaluating the Options

  • A. After the $i$-th iteration, the last $i$ elements of the array are in their correct sorted positions.

    • TRUE.

    • In the 1st iteration ($k=n$), the global maximum is found and moved to position $n$. The last 1 element is now sorted.

    • In the 2nd iteration ($k=n-1$), the next largest element is found and moved to position $n-1$. The last 2 elements are now sorted.

    • By induction, after the $i$-th iteration, the largest $i$ elements have been moved to the suffix of the array in sorted order.

  • B. In each iteration, the algorithm always requires exactly 1 flip in the worst case.

    • FALSE.

    • In the worst case (e.g., the maximum element is in the middle of the prefix), 2 flips are required: one to bring it to the top (front) and one to move it to the correct end position.

    • It requires 1 flip only if the maximum is already at the front. It requires 0 flips if the maximum is already at the correct end position. Since the worst case is 2, the statement "exactly 1" is incorrect.

  • C. In the worst case, the total number of flips performed by the algorithm is at most $2n$.

    • TRUE.

    • The algorithm runs for $k = n$ down to $2$, which is $n-1$ iterations.

    • In each iteration, at most 2 flips are performed.

    • Total flips $\le 2 \times (n-1) = 2n - 2$.

    • Since $2n - 2 < 2n$, the statement "at most $2n$" is a correct upper bound.

  • D. The number of comparisons required by the algorithm is $O(n^2)$.

    • TRUE.

    • To find the maximum in a prefix of size $k$, we perform $k-1$ comparisons.

    • The total comparisons sum up as: $(n-1) + (n-2) + \dots + 1 = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

    • This is a quadratic arithmetic progression, so the complexity is $O(n^2)$.

Conclusion

The correct statements are A, C, and D.
